metadata.title: Teaching with confidence: How a skill-based intervention develops teacher self-efficacy and improves educational outcomes

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study uses an RCT with teacher-level intentional sampling in South Korea (102 recruited; 91 completed). The unit of analysis is the teacher, and outcomes include teacher self-report scales and class-average PE grades provided by teachers. The manuscript does not report the use of complex survey sampling weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight procedures; therefore, no population-representative weighting strategy is documented. Analytically, the authors treat missing questionnaire data using Mplus FIML (1.1% missing), standardize variables, and estimate longitudinal mediation within structural equation modeling rather than using PV-based achievement scaling or ILSA survey-weighted estimation.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values are not applicable because the study does not use ILSA-style cognitive achievement PVs; instead, it models teacher self-efficacy/job satisfaction (Likert-type scales) and class-average PE course grades reported by teachers. Missing data handling is implemented via Mplus full information likelihood estimation (FIML) for the CFA/SEM measurement and structural models, which is treated here as multiple-imputation-style handling for missingness under the model-based framework. Because the dependent variables are not PV-based achievement scores, PV handling does not apply to this design.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Teachers were recruited from the population of full-time ethnic Korean PE teachers participating in a required annual national training program in South Korea. Intentional sampling was used: teachers were invited from the training program, and 102 agreed to participate; 11 did not maintain participation during the year-long study. The analytic sample includes the 91 teachers who completed all waves (T1, T2, T3) and all aspects of the study, with each teacher coming from a different school (102 teachers from 102 schools at baseline; 91 persisting teachers from 91 schools). The study reports no additional grade-level or school-type exclusions beyond the teacher-level covariates used in the model (grade level taught and special-needs students in class).

main_findings.dataset_used: South Korea year-long RCT teacher intervention (T1/T2/T3) — PE teacher self-efficacy for student engagement
main_findings.target_variable: T2 teacher self-efficacy (TSE) for student engagement
main_findings.performance_metrics: Structural equation modeling (Mplus 8.3, MLR, FIML). Experimental condition → T2 TSE for student engagement: β = 0.46, SE = 0.09, p < .001. Model fit for hypothesized model: χ2(14)=21.20, p=.10, RMSEA=0.076, SRMR=0.039, CFI=0.982, TLI=0.917.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using the South Korea year-long RCT teacher intervention data (T1/T2/T3) to model teacher self-efficacy for student engagement, the study leveraged experimental condition, baseline TSE, baseline autonomy-supportive teaching, and teacher covariates to predict T2 TSE for student engagement, finding that the intervention significantly increased T2 TSE (β = 0.46, p < .001). This indicates that skill-based autonomy-supportive teaching training can causally strengthen teachers’ confidence in engaging students, supporting the design of teacher professional development that targets domain-specific efficacy beliefs.

main_findings.dataset_used: South Korea year-long RCT teacher intervention (T1/T2/T3) — PE teacher job satisfaction
main_findings.performance_metrics: Experimental condition → T3 job satisfaction (direct): β = 0.08, SE = 0.06, p = .142 (non-significant). T2 TSE for student engagement → T3 job satisfaction: β = 0.20, SE = 0.06, p = .002. Mediation: total indirect effect via T2 TSE for student engagement: β = 0.32, SE = 0.06, t = 5.34, p < .001, 95% CI [0.22, 0.43]; specific indirect via T2 TSE: β = 0.09, p = .008, 95% CI [0.04, 0.15]; T2 AST did not mediate (β = −0.01, p = .608).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using the South Korea year-long RCT teacher intervention data (T1/T2/T3) to model teacher job satisfaction, the study leveraged T2 teacher self-efficacy for student engagement, experimental condition, and baseline/covariate controls to predict T3 job satisfaction, finding that T2 TSE for student engagement significantly increased T3 job satisfaction (β = 0.20, p = .002) and fully mediated the intervention effect (direct effect became non-significant). This indicates that teacher professional development may improve job satisfaction by first building teachers’ efficacy for engaging students, suggesting efficacy-focused training components rather than skill training alone.

main_findings.dataset_used: South Korea year-long RCT teacher intervention (T1/T2/T3) — PE class-average student achievement
main_findings.performance_metrics: T2 TSE for student engagement → T3 student achievement: β = 0.24, SE = 0.08, p = .005. Experimental condition → T3 student achievement (direct): β = −0.06, SE = 0.09, p = .508 (non-significant). Mediation: total indirect effect via T2 TSE for student engagement: β = 0.17, SE = 0.05, t = 3.23, p = .001, 95% CI [0.08, 0.25]; specific indirect via T2 TSE: β = 0.11, p = .011, 95% CI [0.04, 0.18]; T2 AST did not mediate (β = −0.02, p = .353).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using the South Korea year-long RCT teacher intervention data (T1/T2/T3) to model class-average student achievement in PE, the study leveraged T2 teacher self-efficacy for student engagement, experimental condition, and baseline/covariate controls to predict T3 student achievement, finding that T2 TSE for student engagement significantly increased T3 student achievement (β = 0.24, p = .005) and fully mediated the intervention effect (direct effect became non-significant). This indicates that improving teachers’ engagement efficacy through skill-based training can translate into better student achievement outcomes, informing policy to incorporate efficacy-building mechanisms into teacher development programs.

data.outcome_summary: This paper reports a year-long randomized controlled trial in South Korea with 91 full-time PE teachers (91 schools; 48 experimental, 43 control) who completed measures at three time points (T1 baseline in August, T2 end of fall, T3 end of spring). The intervention trained teachers in autonomy-supportive teaching (AST) through three face-to-face sessions, and the study modeled teacher self-efficacy (TSE for student engagement), job satisfaction, and class-average PE grades. Using structural equation modeling in Mplus with MLR and FIML for 1.1% missing data, the experimental condition significantly increased T2 TSE for student engagement (β = 0.46, p < .001). T2 TSE for student engagement then predicted T3 job satisfaction (β = 0.20, p = .002) and T3 student achievement (β = 0.24, p = .005), with full mediation of the intervention effects. Limitations include teacher-report measurement for AST and student achievement, modest sample size for SEM, and no PV-based ILSA achievement framework; thus, results are not directly generalizable beyond PE teachers in this training context.
